doc.title: Neal Caine interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

title: Playing other people's basses with pickups
summary: Using borrowed amplified basses changes his approach; he wants a pretty but nasty sound with no frills.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: What happens when you travel somewhere and you can’t take your own bass?

Well I just deal with — I deal with whatever. I mean I have, I’ll say this, now that happens. And if it’s a bass that’s set up for only an amp, like I’ll try to use it acoustically. But some basses you get and the action is this high, and you literally — so there’s been probably five to ten times where yeah, I’ll go on a gig and I’ve had to play that bas — and you know it is so fucking easy I sound like Miroslav Vitous, I’m playing all types of crazy shit you know, like Niels Orsted Pederson, I’m all — because it changes the way I approach it too. I don’t like it because I like to dig in and swing, and with the pick-up generally, depending on how it’s set up it’s too easy. So it changes my physicality. So the next thing you know, I’m all flowery and shit. Like I don’t like it you know. It’s just not for me.
I like your mix of descriptive terms ‘cause you’ve said “pretty” a few times, but you don’t necessarily like your bass to be [scats] pretty. You want it to have some natural oomph.

Right. Well pretty can be dark and nasty too, I mean it depends on how you mean pretty. I’m not sure which references I was making. But I want it to be pretty but I want it to be nasty and have some depth to it. And not just frilly.
